scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Drumless Beat: How the Juba Dance Survived
This is Juba dance. 18th-19th century.
on_screen: Title card: Juba dance · United States · 18th-19th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated from the Kongo and was brought to Charleston, South Carolina, by enslaved people.
It served as a means of communication and cultural preservation on plantations where drums were prohibited.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a spiritual practice and a method of communication, it evolved into a performance tradition that preserves African American identity and history.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance involves stomping and slapping the body, including arms, legs, chest, and cheeks.
It includes specific steps such as the 'Yaller Cat', 'Pigeon Wing', 'Blow That Candle Out', and concludes with the 'Long Dog Scratch'.
Watch for Yaller Cat, Pigeon Wing, Blow That Candle Out.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The primary instrument is the human body.
Music often features call-and-response chants or songs, with rhythms that simulate the function of talking drums.
Listen for the Body (hands, feet, chest, cheeks).
A percussive soundscape created by the human body, characterized by stomping, clapping, and slapping that mimics the function of talking drums.

scenes.title: The people
narration: William Henry Lane (Master Juba), Florence Price, Bo Diddley.
Known as Giouba or Djouba in Haiti, and practiced in the Caribbean, Suriname (Dutch Guiana), and the United States.
Roots in Kongo spiritual practices; influenced American tap dance, stepping, and the Bo Diddley beat.
